Guinea Energy Intelligence Report 2026 — Intelligence Platform

Guinea Energy Intelligence — Alendei Internal Edition — v1.3 · Power-sector assessment, investment pipeline and priorities for 2027–2035 · 16 October 2026 · Evidence retrieved 08–15 October 2026

Sponsor and preparer: Alendei Green RE Pvt. Ltd. (Alendei Group). Evidence-led research; not a government-approved dataset.

Executive overview

Bottom line. Guinea has a large hydro base (787.7 MW of 1,305.6 MW installed in 2025) and was a net exporter in 2025, a wet year. Its system is not yet firm: there is no documented dry-season dependable capacity, the grid into Conakry is congested, the utility sells at about a third of its cost, and the pipeline is long but thinly committed.

Key findings

  • Rapid growth, fragile firmness. Installed capacity roughly doubled from 593–699 MW reported for 2017 (EDG and World Bank figures differ) to 1,305.6 MW in 2025, and peak served reached 961 MW. The World Bank describes only about 1,000 MW as 'reliably available', a term it does not define, and no seasonal dependable capacity is documented for any hydro plant.
  • Hydrology is the system's swing factor. Konkouré natural flows range from about 18 m³/s in April to 1,250 m³/s in August. The 2024 drought cut hydro output by more than 10%, nearly doubled HFO burn and caused large load shedding. In 2025, a wet year, EDG's summary table shows 903 GWh of exports (unit implied by the country breakdown).
  • The grid into Conakry is a constraint in its own right. Conakry substation transformers ran at about 80–103% loading in EDG's latest published table (2022/2023), and the main reinforcements are financed but slow. Guinea–Mali is about 85% complete on its World Bank-financed works but delayed, and Linsan–Fomi has been financed since 2021 with no works evidenced.
  • The utility is not financially sustainable. The average tariff is about US¢10/kWh against a cost of service of about US¢27/kWh. Subsidies averaged 55% of revenue (2019–2023), IPP payables reached GNF 6,500 bn (2023), and EDG reported a GNF 430 bn loss for 2025 (labelled audited by EDG; no audit opinion retrieved).
  • Demand is rising fast, but mining stays captive. Mining uses about 558 MW of mostly captive generation, and planned refineries come with their own plants. The national plan's 3,894 MW for 2030 includes loads that are not contracted with the grid.
  • The pipeline is long, commitments are short. About 379 MW of new generation (nameplate) is at differing stages: Amaria 300 MW is under construction; Kankan 40 MW, EBID micro-hydro 27.6 MW and Tinkisso 2 11 MW have signed financing but no evidenced construction start. None is commissioned. Only Amaria has a published online year (2027); Kankan's works had not been tendered by January 2026. About 6.5 GW of stated hydro, thermal and solar nameplate sits at active-development, announced or proposed stage (may include duplicate listings; includes Sambangalou, 128 MW, located in Senegal).
  • Financing needs far exceed commitments. The Mission 300 compact needs US$11.47 bn for 2025–2030, of which US$8.90 bn remains to be raised. Its US$2.56 bn 'mobilised' figure mixes signed loans with unsigned items. No energy guarantee has yet been used in Guinea.
  • Resources are large but unequally evidenced. Hydro technical potential is 6,233 MW (atlas). Modelled solar-resource values are withheld from this edition pending licence confirmation. Modelled onshore wind is weak, with no measurements. No source demonstrates commercially viable potential for any technology.

What should Guinea do next? See the National way forward. Alendei's proposed (unapproved) market-entry strategy is in the separate, confidential Alendei strategy tab.

The department's questions

1. What is Guinea's present electricity situation, and what are the principal constraints?

A hydro-dominated system of 1,305.6 MW installed capacity (2025), two-thirds owned by IPPs selling to EDG as single buyer. It supplied a record 961 MW peak and 5,551 GWh in 2025, and EDG's summary table shows 903 GWh of exports (unit implied). The principal constraints are: dry-season firm supply (no documented dependable capacity; the 2024 drought produced large load shedding); an overloaded Conakry transmission and substation network; and a utility that sells at about US¢10/kWh against a cost of service of about US¢27/kWh, with GNF 430 bn of losses (2025) and IPP arrears.

2. How much of the problem concerns generation, dependable capacity, seasonal hydrology, transmission, distribution, utility finances and reliability?

All are binding, in different seasons and places. Annual energy was sufficient in 2025, a wet year with exports. Dry-season firm capacity is not: in 2024 EDG reported 129,797 hours of load shedding for production deficit and 543–794 GWh of unserved energy. Grid constraints persist into Conakry (transformer loading of about 80–103% in EDG's latest published substation table, 2022/2023). Losses are reported at 30% for 2024 (technical and commercial in the Mission 300 compact; theft, non-billing and technical in a World Bank document) and commercial losses at 40% for 2025 (World Bank); the measurement bases are undocumented and the figures are contested (CON-0013). Together with weak collections, they drive the financial gap. The evidence does not allow a quantified share for each factor; a daily load curve and seasonal dependable-capacity data are missing.

3. What demand growth is evidenced for 2027–2030, particularly from mining and industrialisation?

Served peak demand nearly tripled from 334 MW (2017) to 961 MW (2025). The national plan projects 3,894 MW by 2030, including about 1,442 MW of mining and 817 MW of exports, but these loads are not contracted with EDG. Mining today uses about 558 MW of mostly captive generation. Five alumina refineries are targeted for 2030 and are designed with their own power plants, and Simandou's power is captive and undisclosed. Evidenced grid demand growth is therefore strong but uncertain in scale, and industrial loads may stay off-grid without new supply and access arrangements.

4. Which generation, grid, storage and access interventions have the strongest evidence-based rationale?

In order of evidential strength: (i) Conakry and backbone transmission reinforcement already financed (Manéah–Linsan, Linsan–Fomi, Guinea–Mali); (ii) completing Amaria and documenting the Konkouré cascade's dependable output and operating rules; (iii) utility recovery (metering, loss reduction, collection of public-sector arrears, an IPP arrears plan); (iv) firm evening and dry-season capacity, technology-open (flexible thermal, storage, imports, solar-plus-storage); (v) a frequency-containment battery, which a WAPP study sizes at 13.2 MW/1 h for Guinea's regional reserve share (a study recommendation for one grid service, not a solution to dry-season shortfalls); (vi) grid-connected solar with a grid-integration study; (vii) off-grid access through GNEAP-2 and the PNER.

5. What are the major risks to project delivery, financing and energy security?

Execution after financing (Linsan–Fomi financed in 2021 with no works evidenced; PAAEG lots at 0% progress); hydrological and climate variability (2050 hydro output range −30% to +25%); concentration of supply on one river; dependence on imported HFO through a single Conakry depot complex; EDG's finances and arrears; high country risk (OECD class 7, no energy guarantees in use); undocumented PPA currency terms; and opaque financing terms for the largest projects.

6. What should the government prioritise immediately, over the next three years, and through 2035?

Immediately: publish dry-season dependable-capacity and cascade rules, start the delayed financed works, adopt the tariff and arrears plans, launch firm-capacity procurement, and assess the 13.2 MW frequency-reserve battery recommended by the WAPP study. 2027–2029: complete the financed grid backbone and Conakry reinforcement, commission Amaria, procure competitively for solar and storage on a hosting-capacity basis, scale metering and loss reduction, and deliver the GNEAP-2 mini-grids. To 2035: decide the next large hydro on dependable output, transboundary rules and financing, connect mining and refinery loads where economic, and build a sector framework (new electricity law, an operational regulator, a grid code and third-party access).

7. What can government, utilities, private investors and development partners each contribute?

Government: policy and legal framework, tariff path, payment discipline and arrears settlement, land and permits, transparent procurement. EDG: system operation, metering, loss reduction, dispatch of the cascade. The regulator (AREE): tariffs, grid code, licensing. Development partners: concessional finance for grid and access, guarantees (none yet used in energy), preparation facilities and technical assistance. Private investors: IPP generation and storage, EPC and O&M, mini-grid concessions, and mining-load supply, once payment security and procurement frameworks exist.

8. Which projects or intervention categories warrant further feasibility work and due diligence?

Konkouré cascade dependable output; Koukoutamba, Fomi, Kogbédou-Frankonédou and Grand Kinkon (dependable output, transboundary rules, resettlement, financing); the Kamissaya/Kindia 50 MWc solar package (scope and financing contradictory); La Côtière 225 kV; LNG-to-power at Kamsar and the 500 MW LNG plants (announced only); grid or shared supply to mining and refinery loads; storage beyond frequency reserve; wind (no measurements); and the currency and payment security of existing PPAs. See the opportunity register and due-diligence backlog.

National way forward

NATIONAL RECOMMENDATION evidence-based sequencing for Guinea, technology-neutral; the same national findings appear in the Public/Government Edition · EVIDENCE register fact · ESTIMATE derived here · HYPOTHESIS needs further analysis. No generation mix, IRR, tariff or capital cost is estimated. The sponsor's commercial perspective is in the separate Alendei strategy tab.
Strategic thesis. Guinea should establish dependable, deliverable and financially sustainable electricity supply before committing to a predetermined generation mix.
This is a sequencing recommendation drawn from the evidence, not a completed least-cost optimisation. The least-cost generation mix, solar and storage volumes and a project ranking cannot be determined responsibly until plant-level seasonal dependable capacity, an hourly load curve, quantified grid hosting and evacuation limits, and payment-security arrangements exist; none is published today (GAP-0010, GAP-0038, GAP-0098, GAP-0106, GAP-0143).

Six findings that shape the way forward

Transmission execution is binding

Linsan–Fomi was financed in 2021 with no works start evidenced; Manéah–Linsan is 41% disbursed but at 8% site progress; Guinea–Mali is about 85% complete on its World Bank-financed works but delayed; Conakry substation transformers ran at ≈80–103% loading in EDG's latest published table (year 2022 or 2023 ambiguous), and a World Bank mission documents overloaded lines into Conakry.

EVIDENCE [DAT-WS06-00023; DAT-WS23-00008; DAT-WS23-00009; DAT-WS16-00005; DAT-WS06-00026; DAT-WS06-00029; DAT-WS21-00005]

La Côtière: stated purpose and inferred effect

Stated purpose (Mission 300 compact): La Côtière 225 kV is for evacuating Kaléta–Souapiti output and supplying mining companies, with US$771 m still to mobilise; Lot 1 is only 'under consideration' by UK Export Finance and no commissioning date is published. Research-team inference: until it is built, the evacuation constraint may limit how much existing hydro output can reach new loads; this effect has not been modelled.

EVIDENCE + INFERENCE [DAT-WS23-00054; DAT-WS23-00052; DAT-WS23-00053; GAP-0148]

Solar scale-up: grid integration not yet quantified

Modelled solar-resource values are withheld from this edition pending licence confirmation. Grid hosting and evacuation limits are not quantified in the available evidence, and the 2019 World Bank grid-integration study is not available. The compact itself calls for correcting evacuation and stability constraints before absorbing large volumes of intermittent energy. Hosting is one constraint among several: land (largely customary tenure, acquired through public-utility declaration and compensation), payment security, PPA terms and the absence of a competitive procurement framework also bind.

EVIDENCE [GAP-0098; DAT-WS18-00079; DAT-WS21-00003; DAT-WS26-00001; DAT-WS26-00002; GAP-0143]

Storage services differ; seasonal deficits need firm energy

Batteries can provide frequency response (seconds to minutes), short-duration power support (up to about an hour) and daily evening-peak shifting (hours). Multi-day or multi-week energy deficits, such as the 2024 drought (hydro output down more than 10%; 129,797 hours of load shedding for production deficit; 543–794 GWh not distributed, two EDG figures), need firm energy, imports or reservoir management. The 13.2 MW, 1-hour battery is a WAPP/GIZ study recommendation for frequency containment, not an adopted requirement. Illustrative scale only: one full discharge of that battery (≈13.2 MWh) is about 1/41,000 of the lower 2024 unserved-energy figure (542,767.5 MWh); the two quantities measure different things (one cycle versus a year's deficit) and the comparison is not a sizing calculation.

ESTIMATE [DAT-WS05-00114; DAT-WS21-00006; DAT-WS05-00188; DAT-WS10-00050; DAT-WS21-00015; CON-0028]

A few delays outweigh the pipeline size

Within the ≈379 MW subset that is under construction or has signed financing (Amaria 300, Kankan 40, EBID micro-hydro 27.6, Tinkisso 2 11 MW), Amaria accounts for 300 MW, i.e. 79% (300 ÷ 378.6); this is a share of that subset, not of the national pipeline. Amaria is delayed at 61% overall execution. Separately, about 6.5 GW of stated nameplate is listed at active-development, announced or proposed stage: a gross aggregation of listings that may include duplicates and includes Sambangalou (128 MW, OMVG, located in Senegal; ≈6.4 GW without it). It is not expected, commissioned, dependable or available generation, and beyond Amaria none of it has a published commissioning date.

ESTIMATE [DAT-WS20-00204; PRJ-0057; PRJ-0081; GAP-0148]

A first private renewable deal could set the precedent

No grid-connected solar plant operates, Khoumagueli has been delayed since its 2019 concession, no World Bank Group energy guarantee is in use and PPA currency terms are undocumented. A first transparently contracted, bankable private renewable transaction, on-grid or industrial, could establish contract and risk-allocation templates for later investment.

HYPOTHESIS [DAT-WS18-00075; PRJ-0095; DAT-WS24-00078; GAP-0143]

Five national priorities, in dependency order

P1 grid deliveryP2 firm baselineP3 payment security→P4 technology-open procurement→P5 industrial supply and trade
P1

Deliver financed transmission

Complete Linsan–Fomi, Manéah–Linsan and Guinea–Mali; reinforce Conakry substations; close financing for La Côtière, whose stated purpose is to evacuate Kaléta–Souapiti output.

Depends on: Financing largely exists
Decision gate: Works schedules published; contracts awarded; La Côtière financing decided

[OPP-0004; OPP-0005; DAT-WS23-00054]
P2

Establish a firm-capacity baseline

Measure plant-level seasonal dependable capacity (Souapiti, Kaléta, Garafiri, Amaria), adopt cascade operating rules, analyse dry-year hydrology and publish an hourly load curve.

Depends on: Data sharing by EDG and plant companies
Decision gate: Dependable-capacity study and load curve published

[OPP-0001; OPP-0018; GAP-0010; GAP-0106]
P3

Restore payment discipline

Adopt an arrears plan for independent producers, enforce payment of public-administration bills, scale metering and secure guarantees for new contracts.

Depends on: Budget decisions
Decision gate: Arrears plan adopted; guarantee eligibility confirmed

[OPP-0006; OPP-0020; DAT-WS09-00093; DAT-WS09-00079]
P4

Procure capacity technology-open, at least cost

Procure firm evening and dry-season capacity through a technology-open least-cost process, including renewables and storage where grid integration, firmness and price justify them.

Depends on: P2 sizing, P1 evacuation, P3 bankability
Decision gate: Least-cost plan and grid-integration study; transparent tender framework

[OPP-0002; OPP-0008; DAT-WS21-00001]
P5

Decide industrial supply and regional trade

Decide how mines and refineries are supplied (grid, shared or hybrid captive) and how connection costs are shared; strengthen WAPP trade and settlement.

Depends on: P1 (La Côtière), P2
Decision gate: Mining-supply policy; connection-cost rules

[OPP-0013; DAT-WS10-00034; DAT-WS06-00025]

Sequence. P1 and P2 start now and in parallel; P3 runs alongside and is the precondition for private finance; P4 is sized on P2 and limited by P1 evacuation; P5 follows P1 and P2. A fixed national solar, wind, hydro or battery volume should wait for P2 and a grid-integration study (financed projects and the studied reserve battery excepted).

Alendei contribution and market-entry strategy (confidential, proposed)

CONFIDENTIAL — INTERNAL ALENDEI STRATEGY. Not for government-facing or public distribution. PROPOSED STRATEGY — pending owner approval.

Commercial perspective of the sponsor, Alendei Group, kept separate from the national recommendations. It is a PROPOSED strategy pending owner approval, not a corporate decision, not a Government of Guinea recommendation and not an independently approved plan. Alendei's capabilities are company-described (alendei.com, SRC-0414, and the group's own description), India-based and not independently verified. Alendei has no evidenced presence, project, licence, partner, financing commitment or customer commitment in Guinea, and no outreach has taken place.

ALENDEI — PROPOSED

A. Recommended entry model

Proposed entry model: asset-light, partner-led entry, with no equity investment, PPA ownership or utility-offtake exposure for the first project unless further evidence and an explicit owner decision justify a different structure. Two tracks: (1) programme procurement — India Exim–financed solar EPC when a real qualification route opens, and GNEAP-2 participation through a qualified operator as EPC or supply partner; (2) private customers — mining and industrial customer discovery and energy audits first, then customer-funded hybrid EPC.

Plausible for entry

Customer-funded EPC; equipment supply and integration; lender-funded (DFI/LoC) procurement; energy audits and advisory services.

Needs more evidence, capital or capability

Deferred-payment EPC; PPA/OPEX with a third-party financier; joint venture with a developer; equity in a project SPV; long-term energy-service contracts.

ALENDEI — PROPOSED

B. First-wave opportunity assessments

India Exim–financed solar for 7 universities and 200 health facilities

MONITOR — prepare to pursue

US$20.22 m Government of India line of credit (US$14.4 m universities; US$5.82 m health), effective 11-Aug-2021; ≥75% of contract value sourced from India. Exim prequalified four consultants for the DPR and tendering services on 18-Feb-2025 (iDeCK, NTPC, TERI, WAPCOS). No EPC prequalification found on Exim's site on 16-Oct-2026.

Status: Approved, not yet procured at EPC level; DPR appointment and EPC timing NOT VERIFIED — owner confirmation required.
Route: Prime EPC or Indian consortium lead (Exim EPC prequalification normally limited to Indian firms — inference to confirm); partners for water pumping and medical cold chain.
Next: Fortnightly check of Exim LoC and e-procurement pages; owner-authorised enquiry to Exim; assemble the EPC credential pack.
Gate: Bid preparation only when EPC prequalification is published and Alendei meets the criteria alone or as consortium lead.

PARTNER — confirm status first

IDA financing effective 30-Mar-2026. Mining and industrial power — customer discovery and energy audits

PURSUE — validation only

Mining requires about 558 MW, mostly captive. Hybrid precedents: Kiniero (HFO + 21 MWp solar + 5.2 MWh, IPP model) and Bankan (HFO + solar design). Trade press reports an unnamed miner planning solar procurement (30-Apr-2026). No published tender; no customer engaged; willingness to buy not established.

Status: Market hypothesis plus press-reported intent (unverified).
Route: Paid or co-funded energy audits and data reviews → customer-funded EPC; build-own-operate only later with an established IPP or financier.
Next: Target list from public disclosures; customer-discovery framework and data request; partner-led introductions after owner authorisation.
Gate: Feasibility only with 12 months of load data, delivered fuel cost, land, mine life beyond contract tenor, counsel-confirmed legal route and acceptable credit.

4 Requires investment, qualifications or approvalsGuinean legal entity; bonding and insurance; project equity and financing; Exim EPC prequalification.
5 Not currently claimablePresence or any completed project in Guinea or Africa; local partnerships; customer or financing commitments; transmission, large hydro or LNG capability.

Credential evidence the owner must supply

  • Completed project references with MW, value, client, dates and completion certificates
  • Audited financial statements, 3–5 years
  • Contracting entity documents, ownership and beneficial owners
  • Compliance policies; no debarment by any development bank
  • Bank-guarantee, bonding and insurance capacity
  • Any Africa or francophone experience (or confirmation that none exists)
  • Capacity to source ≥75% of contract value from India (Exim LoC)
  • French-language staff or partner plan
  • Approved risk appetite and decision authority

Customer data needed before any proposal

  • 12 months of 15-minute or hourly load
  • Generator fleet, fuel use and delivered fuel cost
  • Grid connection and tariff, if any
  • Outage history; reliability and power-quality needs
  • Remaining operating life
  • Available land and tenure
  • Credit information and payment currency
  • Preferred contract (EPC, OPEX/PPA, build-own-operate)
  • Permits held

D. 90-day plan, screening and decision gates

Days 0–15 · Internal readiness

  • Approve or amend the entry model (D0)
  • Assemble credentials and references (D1)
  • Set risk appetite: EPC-only vs equity (D2)
  • Make/partner list; decision authority
  • Fast-track Exim and GNEAP-2 status check (D3)

Days 16–30 · Verify opportunities

  • Owner-authorised enquiries to Exim and EDG/PAAEG
  • Guinean counsel memo on entity, private supply, local content, GNF (D4)
  • Target customer categories from public evidence
  • Eliminate routes with no credible participation path (D5)

Days 31–60 · Partners and customers

  • Partner long-list and due diligence
  • Customer-discovery framework, NDA, data request
  • Discovery through authorised channels
  • Contracting and financing pathway (A/B/G/H)
  • Concept notes only with real data (D6)

Days 61–90 · Qualify and decide

  • Assess engagement and data
  • Legal and qualification screening
  • Apply the first-project screening framework
  • Bid/no-bid or development memo
  • Leadership decision: proceed, partner, defer or stop (D7)

Power system, hydrology and reliability

Demand, access and scenarios

Demand scenarios for 2030

Scenario2030 MWClassBasis
A. Served-demand trend (illustrative)1,860ESTIMATE2017–2025 compound growth of peak served (14.1% a year, 334 → 961 MW) extended to 2030. Arithmetic illustration only: it ignores suppressed demand, new mining connections and price effects. [DAT-WS10-00013; DAT-WS05-00103]
B. National plan (Plan Directeur, via Mission 300 compact)3,894FORECASTOfficial 2030 power demand, including about 1,442 MW of mining load and 817 MW for interconnection exports. The definition and scope differ from EDG's peak served. [DAT-WS10-00041]
C. WAPP 2019 Master Plan base case (benchmark)—FORECAST666 MW projected for 2025 was already exceeded by 961 MW served in 2025. The WAPP demand definition is not shown to be comparable, so this is not treated as a forecast error; the 2019 vintage predates the 2024–2025 surge. [DAT-WS10-00039]

Supply-side reference points: 1,305.6 MW installed (2025); about 1,000 MW 'reliably available' (World Bank, undefined); about 379 MW nameplate at differing stages: Amaria 300 MW under construction, and Kankan 40 MW, EBID micro-hydro 27.6 MW and Tinkisso 2 11 MW with signed financing but no evidenced construction start. None is commissioned, and only Amaria has a published online year (2027, compact; first 100 MW unit targeted Aug-2027, press). The 1,000 MW figure is not a firm-capacity measure, so no reserve margin can be derived from it. Seasonal dependable capacity is not documented for any hydro plant, so a firm capacity balance cannot yet be computed (data gap GAP-0010, GAP-0038, GAP-0106).

Priorities and roles

Immediate (next 12 months)

  • Commission a Konkouré cascade dependable-capacity and operating-rules study (Souapiti, Kaléta, Garafiri, Amaria) and publish dry-season firm output.
  • Unblock financed works: Linsan–Fomi, Manéah–Linsan, Kankan 40 MW tender, PAAEG lots. Publish a works schedule for each.
  • Adopt and implement the compact's IPP-arrears repayment plan and a public-administration payment discipline for EDG bills.
  • Launch technology-open procurement for firm evening and dry-season capacity, sized on a published load curve.
  • Assess a frequency-containment battery: a WAPP/GIZ study recommends 13.2 MW, 1 hour for Guinea's share of regional primary reserve. It serves one grid service and does not address dry-season energy shortfalls.
  • Publish a daily load curve and reconcile 2024 billed energy and unserved energy (open contradictions).

Next three years (2027–2029)

  • Complete Conakry reinforcement (Manéah–Linsan, Matoto–Manéah, northern 225 kV loop) and the Guinea–Mali and Linsan–Fomi lines.
  • Commission Amaria with its evacuation and integrate it into cascade operation.
  • Run a grid-integration and hosting-capacity study, then procure grid solar competitively, paired with storage where firmness requires it.
  • Scale prepaid and smart metering, cut technical and commercial losses, and move to a cost-reflective tariff path with social protection.
  • Deliver the GNEAP-2 mini-grids and the PNER off-grid programme, with a mini-grid regulation and subsidy window.
  • Relocate fuel storage (Moribaya depot) and publish delivered fuel costs to EDG and mines.

Strategic direction to 2035

  • Select the next large hydro (Koukoutamba, Fomi, Kogbédou-Frankonédou, Grand Kinkon) on dependable output, basin rules, resettlement and financing.
  • Develop supply arrangements for mining and refinery loads (grid, shared or hybrid captive) where economic and reliable.
  • Adopt the new electricity framework law, make AREE operational, publish a grid code consistent with REMC-WA, and define third-party access.
  • Strengthen regional trade within WAPP and secure the transmission-fee settlement mechanisms (OMVG, CLSG).
  • Build hydrological monitoring and climate-risk management into planning (CMIP6 range −30% to +25% hydro output by 2050).

Method and limitations

  • Research was carried out in four evidence batches covering 26 workstreams, 08–15 October 2026. Verification status: research, data extraction and drafting followed an approved research protocol and were directed and reviewed in batches by the sponsor's project owner. Extracted figures were checked against the retrieved source text within that process; they have not been independently verified by a human subject-matter expert, formally accepted or adversarially reviewed.
  • Sources follow a six-tier hierarchy: 1 Guinean official; 2 regional bodies; 3 DFIs, IMF, UN; 4 data institutions and peer-reviewed research; 5 company disclosures and press (issuer's own facts only); 6 leads, never evidence.
  • Evidence states: VERIFIED (tier 1–3, exact), CORROBORATED (two independent sources), EXTRACTED/INDICATIVE (tier 4–5 or unclear definition), ESTIMATE (derived, method stated), CONTRADICTED_UNRESOLVED.
  • Capacity classes (installed, available, dependable, dispatched) and energy classes (generated, delivered, billed, consumed) are kept distinct; PV capacity states MW-DC or MW-AC.
  • Project stages follow evidence: proposed, announced, active development, financially committed, under construction, operational. A memorandum or announcement never counts as a commitment.
  • Financing amounts carry milestones: requested, announced, approved, signed, effective, disbursed, expended, estimated cost.
  • All register records are PROPOSED. Evidence acceptance (Gates 3–4) has not yet taken place, and figures should be read with their stated confidence.
  • Version 1.3 presents national findings, priorities and a roadmap with a sponsor disclosure. National priorities are sequencing recommendations, not a least-cost optimisation. No generation mix, IRR, tariff or capital cost is estimated.

Personal names in three source titles have been replaced by roles. Legal, financial, tariff and regulatory content: verify with a qualified professional before acting.
